DRS Adapter Analysis — Executive Summary

Generated: 2026-04-18  |  Author: Kevin R. Roy  |  Reads sampled: 100,000 per dataset (reservoir sampling from BAM)  |  Adapter regex: T[CT]{0,10} (empirically derived)

Key finding: After trimming the DNA adapter residual from the 3′ end of each read and measuring poly(A) from the remaining basecalled sequence, ≥96% of DRS reads carry at least 1 bp of poly(A) (98–99% in WT samples; lower in CPA-depletion mutants and MinKNOW-basecalled samples). Reads ending in clean poly(A) tails were presumably trimmed completely by Dorado's adapter removal; only reads where trimming was partial retain a residual stub. We infer that this stub is a basecalling artifact — the RNA-trained model's decoding of the remaining DNA adapter signal — because it follows the stereotyped pattern 5′-T[CT]+ consistent with the adapter sequence, not biological RNA. The Dorado pt:i: tag (raw signal-level estimate) is systematically ~33–73% longer than the sequence-derived poly(A) length (a median offset of ~5–11 bp) and shows a modest positive correlation with sequence-based length (Pearson r ≈ 0.22–0.33 across datasets).

1. Experimental Overview

Four DRS datasets (ONT SQK-RNA004, yeast S. cerevisiae) were analyzed:

  • Anchor-away — 9 BAMs: prp28, rrp6, sen1, sen1rrp6 (2–3 reps each)
  • by4742/dst1 — 15 BAMs: dst1Δ, ski2Δ, ski7Δ, upf1Δ, WT (3 reps each)
  • CPA depletion (PRJNA1229592) — 9 BAMs: rna15, ysh1, WT (3 reps each)
  • TFIIIB depletion (PRJNA1368869) — 3 BAMs: wt_tfiiib (3 reps)
⚠️ dst1Δ technical note: The three dst1d_rep BAMs were generated by MinKNOW v6.8.11 live basecalling, whereas all other by4742 samples were basecalled with Dorado 1.3.1 HAC using --estimate-poly-a. MinKNOW's older basecaller produces lower apparent poly(A) detection rates. This is a technical artifact, not a biological difference.

2. Poly(A) Detection Summary

Algorithm

  1. Orient every read to RNA 5′→3′ (minus-strand reads are reverse-complemented)
  2. Examine the last 150 bases (the 3′ tail region)
  3. Pass-1 adapter trim: match T[CT]{0,10}$ at the 3′ end and remove the matched bases. This captures the most common Dorado trimming residual.
  4. Strict 3′-anchored poly(A) scan: scan right-to-left from the actual end of the trimmed sequence using a pure-A (max_error_rate = 0.0) criterion — the scan stops at the first non-A base encountered. A read ending in G or C immediately returns poly(A)=0 (≠ the old "rightmost A" approach which could find isolated A's anywhere in the window). Strict mode is used because permissive scanning (≤15% non-A) over-trims 84% of reads by bridging internal T's into upstream genomic A-tracts; any ambiguous boundary is left for post-alignment resolution with genomic context. Consequence: if any non-A base remains at the very 3′ end of the trimmed sequence — because the adapter stub was not fully removed — the scan terminates immediately and returns poly(A)=0 or a very short count. This is the dominant explanation for the sub-10 nt population visible in the empirical histogram: those reads are not genuine 1–9 nt poly(A) tails (which could not have been captured by oligo-dT hybridisation requiring ≥10 A's), but rather reads where residual adapter bases at the 3′ end truncate the scan prematurely. The Dorado pt:i: tag is unaffected by this because it is computed from the raw signal independently of basecalling.
  5. Pass-2 adapter trim (if scan returns 0 and last base ≠ A): iteratively peel 1–15 bases from the 3′ end; at each step where the new end is A, check for poly(A) ≥ 5 bp. The peeled stub must contain a T, which marks the poly(A)/adapter boundary. This rescues reads where the adapter stub contains an A basecalling error (e.g., TACC instead of TCC) or a G from deeper in the GGCTTCTTCTT adapter.
Why two passes? Dorado pre-trims high-confidence adapter matches from the 3′ end. What remains in the basecalled read is a short residual stub at the poly(A)/adapter boundary — what the RNA-trained model decoded from the DNA adapter signal. The most common residual is T[CT]+ (pass 1). A minority of reads carry a slightly longer or more complex residual that includes G or an A basecalling error, reflecting deeper decoding of the GGCTTCTTCTT adapter sequence (pass 2). Requiring T in the pass-2 stub distinguishes adapter residuals from reads that genuinely terminated in non-A gene body sequence.

Adapter pass breakdown (all datasets combined, 400k reads)

1 — T[CT]+~183k45.7%Common Dorado residual stripped by pass-1 regex

Remaining poly(A)=0: 2.1% of reads — these end in C or G with no T-containing stub, indicating the read genuinely terminated in the gene body before reaching the poly(A) tail.

3. Poly(A) Length Distributions

Per-sample poly(A) violins — empirical (seq) and Dorado pt:i: signal estimate

Each violin shows the distribution of poly(A) lengths per sample. Top panel: empirical poly(A) (basecalled sequence, after adapter trim). Bottom panel: Dorado pt:i: tag (raw signal-level estimate). The pt:i: estimate is systematically longer — it is a raw-signal-level measurement computed independently of basecalling; the poly(A)/adapter boundary region may contribute current that the signal detector includes in the poly(A) estimate. The two measurements show a modest positive correlation (Pearson r ≈ 0.22–0.33). ⚠️ dst1d samples used MinKNOW — lower seq poly(A) lengths are a basecalling artifact, not biology (see Section 1 note).

Poly(A) length distribution by dataset

Density distributions of empirical poly(A) length (left) and Dorado pt:i: tag (right) across all four datasets. CPA-depletion samples (PRJNA1229592) show broader poly(A) tail distributions, consistent with altered 3′ processing.

Red dotted line at 10 nt — oligo-dT hybridisation minimum. The SQK-RNA004 protocol captures RNA molecules by annealing an oligo-dT primer to the poly(A) tail. Stable hybridisation requires a minimum of ~10 consecutive adenosines; shorter tails cannot be efficiently captured. Consequently, reads with an empirical poly(A) length below 10 nt should not be present in a correctly prepared library, and the percentage shown to the left of the line is interpreted as a scan artifact fraction rather than a genuine biological signal (see algorithm step 3 above). The same reference line is drawn on the pt:i: panel for comparison: the pt:i: tag is computed from the raw ionic-current signal independently of basecalling and is therefore not subject to the same premature-termination artifact. A meaningful sub-10 nt fraction on the pt:i: side would indicate a genuine library-preparation problem; in practice the signal-level estimate places very few reads below this threshold, consistent with the artifact interpretation on the sequence side.

4. pt:i: Tag vs. Empirical Poly(A) Correlation

The Dorado pt:i: tag is a raw-signal-level poly(A) estimate computed independently of basecalling. It is systematically longer than the sequence-derived poly(A) length (median offset ~5–11 bp across datasets), likely because the poly(A)/adapter boundary region contributes current that resembles poly(A) signal. The two measurements show a weak but consistent positive correlation (Pearson r ≈ 0.22–0.33; Spearman ρ typically higher — see table). The low Pearson r is expected: a Dorado pt:i: detection floor of ~5–6 bp and sequence-side homopolymer undercalling both compress the distributions near their modes, attenuating linear correlation.

Our pt:i: medians of ~20–26 nt are per-read medians (median of individual pt:i: values across all reads, no gene stratification). Published yeast reference values for context — with per-read vs. per-gene weighting flagged where ambiguous:

  • Tudek et al. 2021 (DRS + Nanopolish, S. cerevisiae; Nat. Commun., PMC8367983): WT poly(A)+ RNA — "mean and median poly(A) tails of 40 and 37 As"; highly expressed mRNAs — "mean of 30 As and a median of 26 As"; newly transcribed mRNAs — mean ~50 nt, max ~200 nt; ncRNA tails — 20–60 nt. The phrasing "mean and median poly(A) tails" reads as per-read, but the paper does not say so explicitly. Their Fig. 3C is unambiguously per-gene (each dot = one gene, r ≈ −0.54 anti-correlation with abundance), with the highest-expressed genes clustering at ~25–35 nt per-gene mean.
  • Begik et al. 2023 (Nano3P-seq, cDNA end-capture; Nat. Methods, PMC9834059): yeast median 23.5 nt, citing Fig. 3d. That figure shows both per-read (left panel) and per-gene median (right panel) distributions; which panel the 23.5 nt references is not specified in the body text. Nano3P-seq's end-capture design avoids the adapter-trim boundary problem entirely, making it a useful independent reference.

Because our statistic is per-read and the weighting of the published numbers is ambiguous, a direct numerical comparison is not yet apples-to-apples. Two mechanistic explanations are plausible and not mutually exclusive: (1) Mass bias: DRS libraries over-represent highly expressed genes; those carry shorter tails (~26 nt median per Tudek), pulling the per-read median down without any basecaller error. (2) HAC basecaller undercount: Dorado Issue #1131 documents indel artifacts in the poly(A) region under the HAC model (strided blocks producing spurious poly-A bases at the tail/adapter boundary), which could bias pt:i: estimates downward. This is orthogonal to mass bias. The clean diagnostic is a per-gene scatter of pt:i: vs. log₂ read count: if it reproduces Tudek's r ≈ −0.54 anti-correlation at matched y-axis range (~25–35 nt for abundant genes, ~40 nt for the bulk), Dorado is accurate at gene level and mass bias explains the low global median; a systematic downshift for matched genes quantifies basecaller undercount. Section 7 shows the per-gene analysis: the two WT-dominated datasets (Anchor-away and TFIIIB depletion) reproduce the negative correlation (r ≈ −0.23 to −0.24), while the two multi-mutant datasets (by4742/dst1, CPA depletion) show near-zero or slightly positive correlations, likely due to condition-level variation dominating over expression rank. The median pt:i: for abundant genes falls ~10–15 nt below Tudek's anchors across all datasets, suggesting a modest Dorado dynamic-range compression on top of mass bias.

Our sequence-based medians (14–16 nt) are lower than pt:i: in all datasets, in the expected direction for homopolymer undercalling; pt:i: is the better proxy. Published benchmarking (Chang et al. 2025, GigaScience, DOI: 10.1093/gigascience/giaf098) compared Dorado pt:i:, nanopolish-polyA, tailfindr, and BoostNano on synthetic RNA of known poly(A) length (Sequins 30 and 60 nt standards); all four tools were within 12% of ground truth across the benchmark, supporting Dorado pt:i: for routine use.

5. DNA Adapter Basecalling Artifact

Background

ONT SQK-RNA004 DRS sequences the RNA molecule 3′→5′ through the nanopore. The molecule structure is:

  5′-[gene body]-AAAAAA…(poly(A) tail)-[DNA adapter: GGCTTCTTCTT…]-3′ ← enters pore first
  (DRS sequences 3′→5′; Dorado outputs reads in 5′→3′ RNA orientation)

Dorado first removes high-confidence adapter matches from the 3′ end of each read during basecalling (RNA adapter trimming cannot be redone post-hoc). For reads where the adapter is fully trimmed, the read ends cleanly at the poly(A) tail (53% of reads). For reads where trimming is partial, a short residual stub remains. Reads ending in clean poly(A) are those where the adapter was fully removed before basecalling; only reads with partial trimming expose remaining adapter signal to the basecaller. We therefore infer that the stub represents the RNA-trained model's decoding of the residual DNA adapter signal. We observe two stub regimes:

  • T[CT]+ residual (46% of reads): The most common pattern. The T at position +1 — consistently observed across all four independent datasets with Dorado HAC basecalling — appears to be a first-characterized feature of the poly(A)/adapter boundary in SQK-RNA004 reads. No prior publication identifies its base identity; the closest prior art is Dorado GitHub Issue #1131, which documents indel artifacts in the poly(A) region under the HAC model (strided blocks producing spurious poly-A bases), confirming that the HAC model is unreliable in this boundary region. The subsequent C/T bases at positions +2 onward most likely reflect correctly called bases from the CTTCTTCTT portion of the adapter (positions 3–11 of GGCTTCTTCTT are natively C and T). Note: all data here used Dorado 1.3.1 HAC; the SUP model reduces but does not eliminate the boundary artifact (Issue #1131).
  • Longer/mixed stub (1% of reads): Reads where the stub contains A basecalling errors or G bases from deeper in GGCTTCTTCTT, e.g., TACC, TG, TAACTG. These are rescued by the pass-2 iterative peel.
Empirically derived adapter regex: T[CT]{0,10}
Derived from reads with confirmed poly(A) ≥ 10 bp: 100% of adapter sequences start with T; subsequent positions are predominantly C or T (A absent; G rare at positions +2–+6 in pass-1 stubs, though G-containing stubs do occur in ~1% of reads and are handled by pass-2). Patterns observed: T (47%), TC (26%), TCC (16%), TCCC (3%), TT (1%), TTC (1%), and other minor variants.

6. Interpretation & Caveats

What the adapter sequence is

The ONT SQK-RNA004 kit uses a DNA reverse transcription (RT) adapter. The relevant strand contains GGCTTCTTCTT at its 5′ end and a dT₁₀ overhang that hybridizes to the poly(A) tail; this strand is what the pore reads immediately after the poly(A) tail (Bauer et al. 2024, Microbiology Resource Announcements, DOI: 10.1128/mra.01041-24). The adapter is DNA, not RNA. Dorado's RNA-trained basecaller encounters the DNA adapter signal and produces a stereotyped residual stub in reads where trimming was incomplete. Because reads with clean poly(A) tails are those where the adapter was fully removed before basecalling, we infer that the T[CT]+ pattern in partially trimmed reads is a basecalling artifact — the RNA-trained model's output when decoding the remaining DNA adapter signal, not the true adapter sequence. We observe this pattern consistently across four independent experiments, confirming it is systematic and reproducible. This is consistent with Dorado GitHub Issue #1131, which documents spurious base emission at the poly(A)/adapter boundary for SQK-RNA004, with the HAC model being more affected than SUP.

Why pt:i: is longer than seq poly(A)

Dorado's signal-level poly(A) estimation (pt:i:) is computed from the raw current trace independently of basecalling. The poly(A)/adapter boundary region may contribute current that the signal detector includes in the poly(A) estimate, as the DNA adapter current can resemble extended dwell at a uniform current level — the same signature used to identify poly(A) signal. This systematic offset (~5–11 bp median across datasets) is consistent across all four datasets and both strands.

Reads without detectable poly(A) (~2.1%)

After adapter trimming and setting min_polya=1, approximately 2.1% of reads show zero basecalled poly(A). These reads are likely: (1) reads from non-polyadenylated RNA species (rRNA, tRNA, snoRNA), (2) degradation products or reads that terminated in the gene body before reaching the poly(A) tail, or (3) reads whose 3′ window is too short to reliably detect poly(A). Breaking this population down by annotated gene class (polyadenylated mRNA vs. non-polyadenylated stable RNA) would distinguish biological from technical origins; this analysis is reserved for future work.

Relationship to published poly(A) estimation tools

Several published tools estimate poly(A) tail length from ONT DRS data and are worth situating against this pipeline:

  • Dorado pt:i: tag — signal-level estimate, used here as reference; see Chang et al. 2025 for benchmarking context.
  • BoostNano (Chang et al. 2025) — a deep-learning poly(A) estimator that tied with Dorado for the best-concentrated distributions in the Chang benchmark on synthetic RNA standards.
  • TAILcaller (Mordziarz et al. 2025, Bioinformatics Advances, DOI: 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf235) — takes Dorado BAM input and supports SQK-RNA004. Closest published tool to this pipeline; the key distinction is that TAILcaller wraps Dorado's pt:i: output, whereas this pipeline derives poly(A) length directly from aligned basecalled bases after a strict 3′-anchored adapter trim.
  • Ninetails (Gumińska et al. 2025, Nature Communications) — identifies non-adenosine residues within the tail (e.g., U, C, G modifications). Orthogonal to poly(A) length estimation; worth integrating as future work if tail composition is relevant to the biology.
  • nanopolish-polyA / tailfindr — signal-level tools benchmarked in Chang et al. 2025; perform similarly to Dorado but require raw pod5/fast5 data. Raw signal is not retained in this study.

7. Per-Gene poly(A) Length vs. Expression

To disentangle mass bias from basecaller undercount, sampled reads were assigned to genes via their splice-alignment coordinates (GFF: saccharomyces_cerevisiae_R64-5-1_20240529; MAPQ ≥ 20; primary alignments only). Per-gene median pt:i: is plotted against log₂(read count) as a proxy for expression level, replicating the diagnostic from Tudek et al. 2021 Fig. 3C (DRS + Nanopolish, r ≈ −0.54). The anti-correlation arises because highly expressed genes are over-represented in DRS libraries and carry shorter poly(A) tails.

Sampling method: Reads are reservoir-sampled directly from BAMs using Vitter's Algorithm R (100k reads per dataset, distributed proportionally across BAMs by read count). Reservoir sampling ensures uniform genome-wide read representation regardless of BAM sort order or chromosome size — unlike the previous stride-5 sequential scan of coordinate-sorted BAMs, which over-sampled reads from early chromosomes (especially chrI) and severely under-counted genes on later chromosomes.

Results (100k reads per dataset, ≥5 reads per gene threshold):

  • Anchor-away (2,699 genes, r = −0.269): negative correlation consistent with Tudek 2021 — highly expressed genes carry shorter poly(A) tails. Weaker than Tudek's −0.54, likely because Dorado pt:i: compresses the dynamic range relative to Nanopolish signal-level estimates.
  • TFIIIB depletion (2,026 genes, r = −0.228): same sign and magnitude as anchor-away; TFIIIB depletion depletes Pol-III transcripts so the gene pool is largely mRNA, yielding a clean negative correlation.
  • by4742/dst1 (1,987 genes, r = −0.237): negative correlation comparable to the WT-dominated datasets. The previous run showed only 109 genes and r = +0.078, an artifact of stride-5 sampling over-representing chrI genes. With proper reservoir sampling, this dataset recovers the expected anti-correlation. It pools five genotypes (dst1Δ, ski2Δ, ski7Δ, upf1Δ, WT); condition-level variation in poly(A) tail length may attenuate but does not reverse the correlation.
  • CPA depletion (2,721 genes, r = −0.174): weaker but still negative correlation. The previous run showed only 232 genes and r = +0.107 — again a stride-5 artifact. The weaker r here (vs. anchor-away/TFIIIB) likely reflects genuine biology: rna15 and ysh1 depletion impairs 3′ cleavage and polyadenylation, introducing heterogeneous 3′ ends that partially decouple poly(A) tail length from expression rank.

The y-axis ranges in all panels (reference lines at 37 nt and 26 nt from Tudek WT and high-expression medians) confirm the signal is on the correct biological scale but globally compressed by ~10–15 nt, consistent with the Dorado pt:i: dynamic-range compression documented in the scatter plots of Section 4.

8. ENO2 Spike-in QC

Each DRS run includes an in vitro-transcribed ENO2 spike-in with a synthetic 3′ UTR (CGTCGTGAGTAGTGAACCGTAAGC) that distinguishes spike-in reads from endogenous ENO2 reads (genomic 3′ UTR: AGTGCTTTTAACTAAGAATTATTAGTCTTT). Reads at the ENO2 locus (chrVIII:451296–452951) are classified by direct 8-mer scanning of the right soft-clip against each UTR sequence (≥2 matching 8-mers required). No A-fraction pre-filter is applied: spike-in reads carry a 24 bp synthetic UTR before the poly-A in the soft-clip, which dilutes the A% below the 50% threshold used by RECTIFY's SpikeInFilter and would cause false-negatives if that pre-filter were active.

Spike-in confirmed datasets: PRJNA1229592_cpa_depletion contains 4,504 confirmed spike-in reads across all 9 BAMs (exhaustive collection of all ENO2-locus reads per BAM), broken down by sample:

The ysh1 replicates 1 and 2 show a ~7-fold spike-in enrichment relative to rna15 and wt (0.74% vs. ~0.10% of ENO2-locus reads). YSH1 encodes the CPA endonuclease (CPF subunit); its depletion may alter the relative abundance or 3′ processing state of endogenous ENO2 vs. spike-in transcripts, or may reflect inter-run library preparation differences. The third ysh1 replicate falls in the normal range (0.11%), suggesting the enrichment in rep1/rep2 is not universal. The spike-in plot below is drawn from this dataset.

inhouse_anchor_away and inhouse_by4742_dst1 each had only 5 spike-in reads across all BAMs (0–2 per BAM), and PRJNA1368869_tfiiib_depletion had 1 — all at noise level. The large ENO2-locus read counts in those datasets (42k–101k reads per BAM) represent endogenous ENO2 expression: one of the most abundantly transcribed genes in yeast.

ENO2 spike-in: pt:i: tag distribution (spike-in vs. endogenous) — CPA depletion dataset

Comparison of Dorado pt:i: (signal-level poly(A) estimate) between confirmed spike-in reads (synthetic 3′ UTR detected) and endogenous ENO2 reads across samples in the CPA depletion dataset. The spike-in was polyadenylated in vitro; differences from endogenous ENO2 poly(A) length reflect the in vitro polyadenylation conditions rather than cellular regulation.
